title: return, not repentance
hook: return, not repentance — you're not lost, you're facing the wrong way
tomorrow: why some prayers need ten people

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yom Kippur, a whole people saying sorry together. Your line was you can start over. Did you take one step toward that apology? Day seventeen.

You're driving somewhere new, and you miss the exit. The map on your phone doesn't lecture you. It doesn't tell you you're a bad driver or that you've ruined the trip. It just says: recalculating. And then, somewhere up ahead: make a U-turn. You were never lost, exactly. You were going the wrong way, and the way back was always there. English has a heavy word for what happens after we do wrong: repentance. It sounds like sackcloth and shame. The Hebrew word underneath it is much closer to that voice on the map. Today: teshuvah.

Teshuvah comes from shuv, to turn, to return. It doesn't say you're broken. It says you're facing the wrong way, and you can turn around. The prophet Hosea calls out, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God." Return. As if home were still there, and it is. The same Hebrew word also means an answer, a reply. Turning around is answering a call. The rabbis thought teshuvah was so basic to the world that they listed it among the things created before the world itself, before anyone had done anything wrong. The way back was built before the road. So how does a person actually turn? Maimonides, in his laws of teshuvah, lays it out plainly. Stop doing the thing. Regret it, honestly. Say it out loud, in words, not just in your head. And decide not to do it again. And then his test for complete teshuvah: you find yourself in the same situation, with the same temptation and the same strength, and this time you don't do it. Not because you can't. Because you've turned. There are two bold teachings about where this leads. One says: in the place where a person who has returned stands, even the completely righteous cannot stand. The one who turned has walked a road the others never had to walk. And another says that when teshuvah comes from love, even deliberate wrongs are transformed into merits, as if the wrong turn became part of the way home. The whole month before the new year, and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, are set aside for exactly this. But the door isn't only open in autumn. It's open today.
screen: `SHUV — TO TURN, TO RETURN.` · `BUILT BEFORE THE WORLD.` · `STOP, REGRET, SAY IT, DECIDE.` · `WHERE THE ONE WHO RETURNS STANDS.` · then, large: `RETURN, O ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: Seventy-five seconds, with the bell. If you can, stand up and slowly turn around, all the way, so you're facing the other side of the room. Then sit. Bring to mind one habit or direction in your life that's pointing the wrong way. Not a verdict on yourself. Just the direction. Picture the U-turn. If you pray, you can ask for help turning. The bell holds the time.
Teshuvah. Return: not shame, but turning around, and answering the call home. Seventeenth word.
Your line: turn around. Today, when you catch yourself heading the wrong way, a sharp word, an old habit, don't beat yourself up. Just make the U-turn. Day seventeen.

howItsDone: Jews focus on teshuvah especially in the month of Elul and the ten days from Rosh Hashanah to Yom Kippur, reflecting on the year, apologizing to people they've wronged and resolving to change, though tradition holds it's possible any day.

fork.setup: a year later you're in the same situation, same temptation, same strength. by Maimonides' test, what makes it complete teshuvah?
options: you don't do it, though you could.
fork.reveal: complete teshuvah: same place, same strength, and this time you don't do it, because you've turned.

original.note: Hebrew: return, from shuv, to turn. it also means an answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: repentance, and feeling bad.
what it means: turning around. you're not lost; you're facing the wrong way, and home is still there.
what a scholar hears: Pesachim 54a lists teshuvah among things made before the world; Maimonides, Laws of Teshuvah 2, gives the steps and the test; Yoma 86b says love turns wrongs into merits.

sources.quoted: Return, O Israel, unto the LORD thy God

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 54a (seven things created before the world)
Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Laws of Teshuvah 2:1–2
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 34b (where the returner stands) and Yoma 86b (from love, merits)

notes: Maimonides' steps are simplified (abandon, regret, verbal confession, resolve); confirm.
'Even the completely righteous cannot stand' (Berakhot 34b) is Rabbi Abbahu's view; Rabbi Yochanan disagrees there. A Keeper may want this noted.
Elul described as 'the whole month before the new year'; confirm.
